Supported Languages

is a framework. It does not depend on reflection, runtime patching, framework lifecycles, or hidden side effects. As a result, works consistently across any environment capable of running TypeScript and JavaScript.

All concepts—FeatureCells, pipelines, reducers, filters, interceptors, lifecycle signals, and immutable state snapshots—are implemented as language-level primitives composed in TypeScript, not framework abstractions.

Any framework integrations exist only as thin adapters that improve ergonomics without changing behavior or rules.

This design allows to serve as a shared foundation for state management across ecosystems. Rather than fragmenting solutions per framework, provides a common core that frameworks can build on together and evolve collaboratively.

What This Means

  • Identical state semantics across all platforms
  • Explicit lifecycle control everywhere
  • No framework lock-in
  • Predictable behavior in any runtime
  • Frameworks add ergonomics, not rules
Core Guarantees (Applies Everywhere)

Regardless of framework or runtime, the following guarantees always hold:

  • FeatureCell identity via a unique string key
  • Explicit FeatureCell registration
  • Explicit initialization (no implicit activation)
  • Deterministic pipeline stages (interceptors → resolve → filters → reducers → taps)
  • Immutable state snapshots
  • Reactive state observation via Observable-based emissions (state$) for snapshot updates
  • Synchronous snapshot access (state) and reactive streams (state$) are both first-class and consistent
  • Well-defined lifecycle signals (reset, destroy, state$, etc.)
  • Strong typing enforced at compile time via generics
  • State evolution follows immutable, reducer-driven semantics aligned with Redux-style principles
  • Tooling- and devtools-friendly architecture with explicit lifecycle and inspectable pipeline stages
  • Extensible by design through composable behaviors and adapters
  • No reliance on decorators unless a platform opts in

These guarantees make  runtime-agnostic by design.

Supported Runtimes & Frameworks
TypeScript-Compatible Environments
Platform Support & Notes
Angular First-class support via @FeatureCell, injectVault, and Angular Signals. Angular adds ergonomic sugar and DI integration on top of the same core runtime but does not alter behavior or lifecycle rules.
Astro Fully supported. Astro's island architecture runs in any framework island (React, Vue, Svelte, Solid) or in standalone TypeScript. FeatureCells persist across page navigations when registered at app scope.
Bun Fully supported with the same semantics as Node.js. FeatureCells function as long-lived stateful services, ideal for orchestration, background processing, and tooling.
Capacitor Fully supported. Capacitor runs web apps in a native WebView. operates identically to a browser environment. Native plugin results integrate naturally via replaceState and mergeState.
Deno Fully supported. Same semantics as Node.js. FeatureCells function as long-lived stateful services, ideal for orchestration, background processing, and tooling.
Edge Runtimes Supported with awareness of runtime constraints. Long-lived FeatureCells may be limited, but request-bounded FeatureCells remain fully valid.
Electron Supported. Combines browser and Node.js runtimes without altering behavior.
Ionic Fully supported. Ionic apps are Angular, React, or Vue apps with a mobile UI layer. works identically to the underlying framework. Mobile lifecycle concerns (background, foreground, offline) are handled explicitly via lifecycle methods.
NativeScript Fully supported. UI layer is irrelevant to ; patterns mirror Angular or React usage.
NestJS Supported with lifecycle awareness. FeatureCells map cleanly to providers.

NestJS-specific notes:
  • initialize() should be called in onModuleInit or onApplicationBootstrap
  • destroy() should be called in onModuleDestroy or beforeApplicationShutdown
  • Singleton-scoped FeatureCells are recommended
  • Request-scoped FeatureCells are generally discouraged
Next.js Fully supported. FeatureCells work in both server components (via server-side state) and client components (via React hooks or direct state access). State registered at module scope persists across navigations.
Node.js Fully supported. FeatureCells function as long-lived stateful services, ideal for orchestration, background processing, event pipelines, CLIs, and servers.
Nuxt Fully supported. Same guarantees as Vue. FeatureCells work in both server and client contexts. State registered via Nuxt plugins persists across navigations.
Qwik Reactivity-first framework. owns state correctness; the framework owns rendering. Strong alignment with fine-grained reactivity.
React Fully supported using plain TypeScript. FeatureCells are registered explicitly and consumed via state, state$, or framework adapters (hooks, external stores). FeatureCells integrate cleanly with React without relying on framework-specific lifecycle assumptions.

React-specific notes:
  • FeatureCells should be registered at application startup (e.g. module scope or app bootstrap), not inside components.
  • initialize() must be called explicitly before state is consumed, typically during application startup or in a top-level provider.
  • State consumption is typically performed via:
    • state$ with subscriptions
    • synchronous state reads
    • framework adapters (e.g. hooks or external store bindings)
  • FeatureCells should not be created per render. They are intended to be long-lived, shared state owners rather than component-scoped objects.
  • Component unmounting does not automatically destroy a FeatureCell. Lifecycle control remains explicit via reset() and destroy().
Service Workers Fully supported with lifecycle awareness. FeatureCells operate within a constrained, event-driven lifecycle governed by the browser. Explicit initialization and destruction are critical, as workers may be suspended or terminated at any time by the runtime.

Best suited for request-bounded or event-scoped FeatureCells rather than long-lived state owners.
Solid Reactivity-first framework. owns state correctness; the framework owns rendering. Strong alignment with fine-grained reactivity.
Svelte Reactivity-first framework. owns state correctness; the framework owns rendering. Strong alignment with fine-grained reactivity.
Tauri Supported. Combines browser and Node.js runtimes without altering behavior.
Vanilla JavaScript Fully supported. FeatureCells operate as plain runtime objects. Explicit initialization and destruction are clearest and most transparent in this environment.
Vue Same guarantees as React. Vue reactivity integrates cleanly via adapters without influencing lifecycle or pipeline semantics.
Web Components Framework-agnostic by nature. FeatureCells may be owned by elements, shared controllers, or host applications without violating any contracts.
Web Workers Fully supported. Web Workers provide a stable, message-driven execution environment well-suited to long-running pipelines. FeatureCells integrate naturally with postMessage-based workflows, where interceptors, filters, and reducers form a deterministic processing pipeline.

Explicit lifecycle control enables predictable teardown and resource management.
Support Language Examples

A FeatureCell is typically declared as an Angular service. The @FeatureCell decorator defines the cell’s identity and state type, while injectVault<T>() retrieves the corresponding vault instance.

The vault must be injected once per FeatureCell and must be stored on the service instance. Injection is synchronous and safe during construction.

What this does

  • Associates the service with a FeatureCell key
  • Resolves the correct FeatureCell vault from Angular DI
  • Provides a fully typed FeatureCell runtime API
  • Ensures the FeatureCell is initialized exactly once

Example: Creating a FeatureCell for Angular

{{`// app.config.ts

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService,
      {
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: [] 
      }
    )
  ]
};
          
// bank-employee.service.ts
// The provideFeatureCell key must match the @FeatureCell key input
          
import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { FeatureCell, injectVault } from '@sdux-vault/angular';
import { Employee } from './employee.shape';

@FeatureCell<Employee[]>('employees')
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class EmployeeService {

  // Use injectVault to get an instance of the FeatureCell
  readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Required to activate the FeatureCell
    this.vault.initialize();
  }
}

// bank-employee.component.ts
@Component({
selector: 'employee-view',
template: \`
  @if (state.hasValue()) {
    <div>
      <p>Employees: {{ state.value() | json }}</p>
    </div>
  }

  @if (state.isLoading()) {
    <div>
      Loading...
    </div>
  }

  @if (state.error()) {
    <div>
      Error: {{ state.error()?.message }}
    </div>
  }
\`
})
export class EmployeeComponent {
  private bankEmployeeServce = inject(EmployeeService);
  state = this.bankEmployeeService.vault.state;
}`}}

Component-Driven UI Frameworks

In component-driven UI frameworks, FeatureCells are not owned by components. Instead, they are registered at application startup and consumed by components as long-lived, shared state containers.

FeatureCells must be created and initialized outside of render functions. Components read state synchronously via state or reactively via state$ or framework-specific adapters (hooks, stores, signals).

What this does

  • Registers a FeatureCell at application scope
  • Initializes the FeatureCell exactly once
  • Allows components to consume state without owning lifecycle
  • Prevents accidental per-render FeatureCell creation

Example: Creating a FeatureCell for a UI Application

{{`// main.ts (or index.ts, app.ts, server.ts, etc.)
import { Vault } from '@sdux-vault/core';

Vault({
  logLevel: 'off'
});
          
// employee.cell.ts
import { provideFeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/core';

export const employeeCell = FeatureCell({
  key: 'employees',
  initialState: []
});

// Explicit activation
employeeCell.initialize();

// --------------------------------------------------
// React / Vue / Svelte / Solid / Qwik components
// consume state but do not own the FeatureCell
// --------------------------------------------------

// employee.cell.ts
const snapshot = employeeCell.state;

// index.ts
const root = document.getElementById('app');

if (snapshot.hasValue) {
  root!.innerHTML = \`
    <h3>Employees</h3>
    <pre>\${JSON.stringify(snapshot.value, null, 2)}</pre>
  \`;
}

if (snapshot.error) {
  root!.innerHTML = \`<p>Error: \${snapshot.error.message}</p>\`;
}

`}}

Web Workers / Service Workers / Edge Runtimes

In worker and edge environments, FeatureCells act as message-driven state pipelines. They receive input via events or messages, process updates deterministically, and emit results explicitly.

There is no UI lifecycle. FeatureCells are created per worker scope or per request boundary, initialized explicitly, and destroyed when the worker or execution context ends.

What this does

  • Creates a deterministic state pipeline inside a worker
  • Processes incoming messages through the full SDuX pipeline
  • Maintains explicit lifecycle control
  • Avoids framework or DOM dependencies entirely

Example: FeatureCell Inside a Worker

{{`// worker.ts

import { Vault } from '@sdux-vault/core';

Vault({
  logLevel: 'off'
});

import { provideFeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/core';

const cell = provideFeatureCell({
  key: 'worker-state',
  initialState: { count: 0 }
});

Cell.initialize();

self.onmessage = (event) => {
  Cell.mergeState(event.data);

  self.postMessage(Cell.state.value);
};

self.onclose = () => {
  // Optional cleanup when worker terminates
  Cell.destroy();
};`}}

Examples: Plain Runtime & Backend

In plain runtime environments, FeatureCells operate as long-lived, stateful services. They are created at process startup, initialized explicitly, and participate in application workflows until shutdown.

This pattern is ideal for servers, background workers, CLIs, orchestration logic, and event-driven systems where deterministic state evolution is required.

What this does

  • Creates a long-lived FeatureCell at process scope
  • Uses explicit initialization and shutdown
  • Supports background workflows and orchestration
  • Requires no framework or platform-specific integration

Example: FeatureCell in a Backend Service

{{`// server.ts
import { Vault } from '@sdux-vault/core';

Vault({
  logLevel: 'off'
});

import { provideFeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/core';

const jobCell = provideFeatureCell({
  key: 'jobs',
  initialState: { processed: 0 }
});

// Activate once at startup
jobCell.initialize();

// Application logic
jobCell.mergeState({ processed: 1 });

// Graceful shutdown
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  jobCell.destroy();
});`}}

Desktop & Mobile Runtimes

In desktop and mobile runtime environments, FeatureCells operate identically to browser or Node.js environments. runs inside the WebView (Capacitor, Electron, Tauri) or alongside the native UI layer (Ionic, NativeScript) without modification.

Mobile lifecycle concerns — background/foreground transitions, offline state, and limited memory — are handled explicitly via lifecycle methods (initialize, reset, destroy).

What this does

  • Runs inside native WebViews or alongside native UI
  • Uses the same FeatureCell APIs as browser environments
  • Handles mobile lifecycle explicitly via destroy() and reset()
  • Native plugin results integrate via replaceState and mergeState

Example: FeatureCell in a Mobile/Desktop App

{{`// app.ts (Capacitor / Ionic / Electron / Tauri / NativeScript)
import { Vault } from '@sdux-vault/core';

Vault({
  logLevel: 'off'
});

import { FeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/core';

const settingsCell = FeatureCell({
  key: 'app-settings',
  initialState: { theme: 'light', notifications: true }
});

settingsCell.initialize();

// Respond to native plugin results
async function onCameraCapture() {
  const photo = await Camera.getPhoto();
  settingsCell.mergeState({ lastPhoto: photo.path });
}

// Handle app lifecycle
document.addEventListener('pause', () => {
  // App entering background — persist or cleanup
});

document.addEventListener('resume', () => {
  // App returning to foreground
});

// Graceful shutdown
window.addEventListener('beforeunload', () => {
  settingsCell.destroy();
});`}}

Meta-Frameworks (Server + Client)

In meta-frameworks like Next.js and Nuxt, FeatureCells bridge server and client execution contexts. state registered at module scope persists across page navigations and works in both server components and client components.

FeatureCells should be registered once at application scope (e.g., in a plugin, layout, or module initializer) and consumed by components via the framework's standard patterns (React hooks for Next.js, Composition API for Nuxt).

What this does

  • Registers a FeatureCell once at application scope
  • Works in both server and client rendering contexts
  • State persists across page navigations
  • Integrates with framework-specific patterns (hooks, plugins)

Example: FeatureCell in a Meta-Framework

{{`// lib/cells/user.cell.ts (shared module scope)
import { Vault, FeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/core';

Vault({ logLevel: 'off' });

export const userCell = FeatureCell({
  key: 'user',
  initialState: { name: '', role: 'guest' }
});

userCell.initialize();

// Next.js: consumed in a client component
// 'use client';
// import { userCell } from '@/lib/cells/user.cell';
// const state = userCell.state;

// Nuxt: consumed via a plugin or composable
// export default defineNuxtPlugin(() => {
//   return { provide: { userCell } };
// });`}}
Summary

is not an Angular library, a React pattern, or a framework-specific solution.

It is a language-level, runtime-level state architecture with optional framework adapters. Frameworks change how you register, consume, and wire FeatureCells—but they never change:

  • Ownership rules
  • Deterministic execution
  • Immutability guarantees
  • Pipeline semantics
  • Lifecycle meaning

This makes suitable for shared, long-term, cross-ecosystem collaboration—exactly as intended.
